en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Ovādavagga 24.
The Training Rule on Material Goods.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the elder bhikkhus, while exhorting the bhikkhunīs, were receiving gains of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
The group-of-six bhikkhus said this:
"The elder bhikkhus have not become so busy with their duties as to exhort the bhikkhunīs; rather, the elder bhikkhus exhort the bhikkhunīs for the sake of material gain."
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... they complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the group-of-six bhikkhus speak thus:
‘The elder bhikkhus are not many in their efforts to exhort the bhikkhunīs; the elder bhikkhus exhort the bhikkhunīs for the sake of material gain’? ...pe...
“Is it true, monks, that you say this:
‘The elder monks do not exhort the nuns because they have done much; the elder monks exhort the nuns for the sake of material gain’?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, speak thus:
‘The elder bhikkhus do not exhort the bhikkhunīs because they have performed much [meritorious work]; the elder bhikkhus exhort the bhikkhunīs for the sake of material gain’?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘If any monk should say, “The elder monks teach the nuns for the sake of material gain,” it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).’”
"But whoever" means whoever such as this...
"a bhikkhu."
...pe... this is the meaning of "bhikkhu" intended here.

"For the sake of material things" means for the sake of robes, almsfood, lodgings, medicinal requisites for the sick, for the sake of honor, for the sake of respect, for the sake of esteem, for the sake of salutation, and for the sake of worship.
"Should speak thus" means:

desiring to bring disrepute upon, desiring to bring infamy upon, or desiring to cause embarrassment to a fully ordained monk who has been appointed by the Saṅgha as a teacher of the nuns, one speaks thus:
"For the sake of robes, for the sake of almsfood, for the sake of lodgings, or for the sake of medicinal requisites for the sick..."
If one says, “He exhorts for the sake of honor, for the sake of respect, for the sake of esteem, for the sake of veneration, or for the sake of worship,” there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If it is a legitimate legal act (dhammakamma) and one perceives it as such, and one speaks thus, there is an offense of expiation.
If it is a legitimate legal act and one is uncertain of it, and one speaks thus, there is an offense of expiation.
If one perceives a legitimate legal act as an illegitimate legal act and speaks thus, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If, desiring to bring disrepute upon, desiring to bring infamy upon, or desiring to cause embarrassment to a monk who has been fully ordained but not authorized by the Saṅgha as an instructor of bhikkhunīs, one speaks thus—saying, "He instructs for the sake of robes...
[and so on] ...for the sake of honor"—there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If one, wishing to speak dispraise, wishing to bring infamy, or wishing to cause embarrassment toward a person who has not been fully ordained—whoever has been appointed or not appointed by the Saṅgha as an instructor of bhikkhunīs—says:

"He instructs for the sake of robes, for the sake of almsfood, for the sake of lodgings, for the sake of medicinal requisites for the sick, for the sake of honor, for the sake of respect, for the sake of esteem, for the sake of veneration, or for the sake of worship," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure (adhamma-kamma) and one perceives it as a legitimate legal procedure (dhamma-kamma), there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as such, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense—

If one speaks while teaching out of natural inclination for the sake of robes, almsfood, lodgings, medicinal requisites for the sick, or for the sake of honor, respect, esteem, veneration, or worship,
except in the case of one who is insane or an initial offender.
The fourth training rule on material things is concluded.
